analysis.one_liner: Raises Medicaid pay for rural hospitals to keep maternity wards open.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by the Senate Finance Committee's own chair and 19 senators, the bill was referred to that committee and died there without a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Keeping Obstetrics Local Act would force Medicaid to pay rural and safety-net hospitals at least 150% of the Medicare rate for maternity and delivery care, with the federal government covering the entire increase, and would send large annual "anchor payments" to small hospitals to keep labor and delivery units running. It would also require every state to give pregnant women on Medicaid a full year of postpartum coverage, and require hospitals to warn communities 180 days before closing an obstetric unit. It never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Pregnant women on Medicaid and CHIP — who pay for roughly half the births in the country — especially in rural areas where hospitals have been closing obstetric units. The bill targets hospitals where at least half of births are covered by Medicaid, CHIP, Medicare, the Indian Health Service, or uninsured patients, so the money is aimed directly at the places serving low-income mothers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicaid to pay eligible rural and safety-net hospitals at least 150% of the Medicare rate for maternity, labor, and delivery services starting in fiscal 2026, instead of the often below-cost rates states currently pay.
Has the federal government pay 100% of the cost of the payment increase, so states don't have to choose between their budgets and their maternity wards.

Requires every state to make an annual anchor payment to small hospitals (under 300 births a year) — starting at $10,000 per delivery plus $1.2 million for standby staffing and equipment — in exchange for a binding contract to keep providing labor and delivery services for at least three years, with the state able to recover the money if the hospital closes.

Makes the full 12-month postpartum Medicaid coverage period mandatory in all states; today states may adopt it but are not required to, and coverage gaps after childbirth are a documented risk period for maternal death.
Requires hospitals to give 180 days' advance notice before closing an obstetric unit and to report cost and closure data publicly, so communities are not blindsided.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the new cost: 100% federal matching for the higher hospital payments, the anchor payments, a $150 million-a-year boost for the Public Health Service Commissioned Corps, and grants for small hospitals to compile cost data. States face administrative work but the federal match shields them from most of the cost of the increase. Medicaid managed care insurers would have to pass the higher rates through to hospitals.

drawbacks.text: The price tag is substantial and open-ended: paying 150% of Medicare rates with a 100% federal match, plus $10,000 per delivery and $1.2 million per hospital in standby payments indexed to medical inflation, commits the federal government to a large recurring obligation without a stated funding source.

Paying a fixed $1.2 million standby fee to every hospital delivering fewer than 300 babies a year is an expensive way to preserve access; critics could reasonably argue that regional centers with good transport would serve some of these communities at lower cost, and the bill does not test that alternative.

Mandating that every state provide 12-month postpartum coverage and minimum payment rates removes state flexibility, and states that would have chosen not to expand are compelled to accept a federal standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real money for real access: maternity wards in rural America are closing because Medicaid pays less than it costs to keep a labor and delivery unit staffed around the clock, and this bill attacks that math directly with federal money and enforceable contracts. The cost is high and the design is generous to hospitals, but it is paired with accountability — states can claw back payments from hospitals that shut down or divert the funds. On the evidence in the bill text, the benefits to mothers in maternity care deserts plausibly outweigh the fiscal cost; what the bill lacked was not a good argument against it but a committee willing to examine it.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Senate Finance Committee — whose chairman was the bill's own sponsor — it sat without a markup, hearing, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, in the closing months of the 118th Congress, joined by 18 fellow Democrats as original cosponsors.
The bill gathered 19 total cosponsors, all Democrats or independents — 18 Democrats and 1 independent — with no Republican support.
On the day of introduction, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance; the action history shows no markup, hearing, or vote ever followed.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it, never reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: rural and safety-net hospitals continue to be paid below-cost Medicaid rates for maternity care, maternity units keep closing without 180-day notice to communities, and taxpayers are not on the hook for the new federal spending. Medicaid managed care insurers are spared a new obligation to pass higher rates through to hospitals.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo holds; maternity deserts persist

against.name: Senate Finance Committee

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and with no votes ever held there is no roll-call record of opposition.

industries.note: The bill would lift Medicaid maternity payment rates to 150% of Medicare and add per-delivery and standby payments worth over $1.2 million a year to small hospitals, in exchange for enforceable contracts to keep labor and delivery open. Hospitals profit, but the public's interest in local maternity care runs in the same direction, and the bill lets states recover payments from hospitals that close.

The bill amends the managed care rules so these insurers must ensure hospitals get the higher minimum rates for maternity care, squeezing their margins on maternity services. Their interest in minimizing hospital payments runs against the bill's goal of adequately paying the hospitals their members give birth in.

industries.industry: Doulas, midwives, and maternal health workers
industries.note: The bill directs HHS to issue guidance on Medicaid and CHIP coverage of doula and midwife services and streamlines enrollment of out-of-state maternity providers, opening paid Medicaid work to a largely community-based workforce.

The bill funds the payment increases with a 100% federal match, a $150 million annual Commissioned Corps authorization, and grants, a large new recurring federal obligation. Whether that is a cost or an investment depends on the value placed on keeping rural maternity wards open.
